title: CheckedSQL — project film
author: Yuhao Fu
narrator: Yuhao Fu, first person (Kokoro am_michael, a neutral local voice; not the instructor persona)
brief: Course email 'What your project film needs to show' (2026-11): four parts in order: executive summary, introduction (what others have done), methods, evaluation.

beats.narration: When you ask an AI to write SQL, you get a query that looks right. My project, CheckedSQL, tells you when it isn't. It takes the AI's query, runs it on a real database, and compares the answer with one I checked by hand.
beats.visual: Question bubble → SQL card with a check that turns into a question mark → database → two answers side by side, one marked wrong.
beats.label: constructed

beats.narration: Why would anyone care? A wrong query doesn't crash. It returns a number that looks just as confident as the right one. CheckedSQL makes those mistakes visible, and it goes one step further: it checks whether the checker itself can be fooled.
beats.visual: Two identical-looking result cards, one secretly wrong; a magnifier finds it; then the magnifier turns to look at the checker box.
beats.label: constructed

beats.narration: Others have built big benchmarks for this. Spider, from 2018, has about ten thousand questions over two hundred databases. BIRD, from 2023, has over twelve thousand on larger, messier data. In BIRD's original paper, ChatGPT got about forty percent right, against ninety-three percent for people.
beats.visual: Two tall stacks of question pages labelled Spider 2018 and BIRD 2023; bars: model about 40 vs people about 93.
beats.label: constructed

beats.narration: Researchers also found that the checker can be wrong. In 2020, Zhong, Yu and Klein showed that running a query on just one database can give a false positive: a wrong query can happen to return the right answer. Their fix was to test each query on many databases.
beats.visual: A wrong SQL card and the gold card both drop into one database and come out with the same result; then several databases appear and the results split.
beats.label: constructed

beats.narration: There are also tools, like the open-source library Vanna, that let you chat with your database and get SQL back. They help you write queries. They don't hand you a record of which answers were wrong.
beats.visual: A chat window sends a question and SQL comes back; an empty results ledger beside it.
beats.label: constructed

beats.narration: So why mine? It isn't a new benchmark, and it isn't more accurate. It's small enough that one person can read every question, check every answer, and rerun everything with one command. And it puts the checker's own blind spots in the results.
beats.visual: A small box beside the big stacks; it opens: twenty pages, a ledger, a rerun loop.
beats.label: constructed

beats.narration: Here's how I built it. The data is Chinook, a free public sample database of a made-up music store. I wrote twenty English questions, and for each one a gold SQL answer, and I checked every gold answer by hand.
beats.visual: The Chinook database with a music note; twenty question pages fan out; each gets a gold card and a hand check.
beats.label: constructed

beats.narration: For each question, the model sees the database schema and a strict contract: reply with exactly one SELECT statement, or the words cannot answer. CheckedSQL checks the contract, runs the query on a read-only copy with a five second limit, and compares the rows with the gold answer.
beats.visual: The pipeline: question → Claude → SQL card through a contract gate → read-only database with a lock and a timer → compare → check or cross.
beats.label: constructed

beats.narration: Then it checks itself. It flags any gold answer that is an arbitrary pick between ties. That happened to me on October twenty-first: four years were tied at eighty-three invoices. And it runs a list of deliberately wrong answers, which should all be caught.
beats.visual: Real screenshot of the 2026-10-21 tie (2009–2012 at 83), outlined; beside it a drawn stack of wrong-answer slips feeding the checker.
beats.label: real screenshot — dated 2026-10-21

beats.narration: Do I have what I need? The code is Python and SQLite, and it's all free. I don't have API credits yet, so this run used Claude Opus five point five inside Claude Code: twenty fresh copies, each seeing only the rules and one question. The API version is built and tested, and it runs with one command once I have a key.
beats.visual: Python and SQLite on a shelf marked free; an API key slot left empty; the Claude mark splits into twenty small cards, one question each.
beats.label: constructed

beats.narration: How will I know it worked? I measure three things: how many answers match the gold answer, how many replies keep the contract, and how many deliberately wrong answers the checker catches. It works if every wrong answer is caught. It fails if a wrong answer can score as right.
beats.visual: Three gauges: match, contract, wrong answers caught; a pass line under the third.
beats.label: constructed

beats.narration: Here's the real run. All twenty answers matched, and all twenty kept the contract. But a perfect score on twenty questions mostly tells me my questions are easy.
beats.visual: Real output of the replay run, 20/20 MATCH, captured 2026-11-24; the final line outlined.
beats.label: real output — captured 2026-11-24

beats.narration: The more useful result: the checker caught seven of eight wrong answers. The one it missed is question sixteen, revenue as price times quantity. Every quantity in this database is one, so a query that forgets it gets the same numbers. That's the false positive Zhong and colleagues warned about.
beats.visual: Real output of check-wrong, 7/8 caught, captured 2026-11-24; the MISSED row for question 16 outlined.
beats.label: real output — captured 2026-11-24

beats.narration: Next, I'll add harder questions and test data where quantities vary, then run it on the API. CheckedSQL: not an AI that's always right, but one whose mistakes you can see. I'm Yuhao Fu.
beats.visual: The pipeline again; new pages join the stack; the cross branch is ringed.
beats.label: constructed
